Noise barriers were eliminated from consideration because barrier aesthetic quality would not be desirable nor complementary to the proposed highest and best use of the land. The proposed highest and best use of the land in the 1990's is expected to be much the same as the land is presently zoned by Cook County and those municipalities involved. The use of structural noise barriers could also instill a feeling of institutionalism to persons viewing abutting residential developments and prospective buyers of undeveloped residentially zoned land.
The majority of the land involved with the proposed improvement is residential, business, and commercial, with lesser quantities of undeveloped lands. The installation of noise barriers would disrupt the view of highway oriented commercial lands from the roadway, the view of the roadway from adjacent lands and the view of lands across the roadway.
Therefore, a more feasible and prudent alternative for reducing a noise impact, is to increase the horizontal distance between the vehicles and the suspected noise susceptible land uses. This requires an evaluation of the situations where it appears that an exception to the standards would be needed because of the economic effect either upon the property owner or the community.
The ability to acquire additional right-of-way as buffer zones and the possibility of altering roadway grades is limited due to the location of the road in relation to the Illinois Central Gulf Railroad overpass, the Cook County Forest Preserve District land in the northwest quadrant of the intersection between Lincoln Highway and Chicago Road, the existing drainage pattern in the area and the extensive residential and commercial developments, long established in the area through which this improvement will pass. Buffer zones could require removal or significant disruption to Section 4(f) lands in the area of Lincoln Highway and removal of residential structures resulting in a severe economic and social hardship on the individual property owners.
